classification.difficultyReason: Construct and graph linear cost and revenue models, then distinguish cakes produced from cakes sold in the giveaway scenario, adjust costs accordingly, and round the paid-sales threshold up to a whole cake.

content.prompt: Bob the Baker wishes to bake and sell cakes. Bob buys the baking equipment for $\$600$. The cost of the ingredients per cake is $\$2$. He then sells each cake for $\$10$. Let $C(x)$ be the cost-function, that shows how much it costs to bake $x$ cakes. Let $R(x)$ be the revenue-function, that shows his gross revenue after selling $x$ cakes.

answer.short: Fixed equipment cost is $\$600$ and ingredients cost $\$2$ per cake, so $C(x)=600+2x$. Sales bring in $\$10$ per cake, so $R(x)=10x$.
answer.worked:
For $x$ cakes, the ingredients cost $\$2x$. Adding the fixed equipment cost gives
$$C(x)=600+2x.$$
Selling $x$ cakes at $\$10$ each gives
$$R(x)=10x.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, determine how many cakes that Bob must sell in order to break even.

answer.worked:
At break-even, revenue equals cost:
$$\begin{align*}10x&=600+2x\\8x&=600\\x&=75.\end{align*}$$
Bob must sell 75 cakes to break even.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Sketch the graph of $y=C(x)$ and $y=R(x)$ on the same set of axes, labelling all important features.

answer.short: $C(x)=600+2x$ has vertical intercept $(0,600)$; $R(x)=10x$ passes through $(0,0)$. The lines intersect at $(75,750)$, for $x\ge0$.
answer.worked:
The cost line has vertical intercept $(0,600)$ and gradient 2. The revenue line passes through $(0,0)$ and has gradient 10. At $x=75$,
$$\begin{align*}C(75)&=600+2(75)\\C(75)&=750\\R(75)&=10(75)\\R(75)&=750.\end{align*}$$
Thus the break-even point is $(75,750)$. Sketch both lines for $x\ge0$, with $x$ representing cakes and $y$ representing dollars.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Suppose that Bob decided to give away the first 10 cakes for free as a way to promote his business. What is the minimum number of additional cakes he must sell to cover all his costs?

answer.short:
78 additional cakes.

The calculated threshold is $77.5$ paid cakes, so round up to the next whole cake.
answer.worked:
Let $n$ be the number of cakes sold after the 10 giveaways. Bob makes $n+10$ cakes, but receives payment for only $n$:
$$\begin{align*}C&=600+2(n+10)\\C&=620+2n\\R&=10n.\end{align*}$$
To cover all costs,
$$\begin{align*}10n&\ge620+2n\\8n&\ge620\\n&\ge77.5.\end{align*}$$
Bob must sell at least 78 additional cakes. Exact zero profit is impossible with a whole number of paid cakes; at 78 paid cakes his profit is $\$4$.
